commitments.claim: Cisco raised its FY2026 hyperscaler AI-infrastructure order expectation to $9 billion and its associated FY2026 revenue expectation to $4 billion.
commitments.horizon: FY2026 conversion and FY2027 backlog carryover

commitments.claim: Management described a major multi-year, multi-billion-dollar campus networking refresh, with campus orders growing more than 25% and data-center switching orders more than 40%.

Cisco announced a restructuring with up to $1 billion of pretax charges, approximately $450 million in Q4 FY2026 and the remainder during FY2027, to support investment in silicon, optics, security and AI.
Long-term product RPO was $11.7 billion, up 6% year over year.

buy_triggers.marker: Reported Q4 FY2026 revenue at or above $16.9 billion, non-GAAP gross margin at or above 66.0%, and FY2027 Q1 revenue guidance of at least $15.6 billion.
buy_triggers.checkable_at: FY2026 results 8-K and earnings release expected August 2026

buy_triggers.marker: FY2027 Q1 product revenue growth of at least 8% year over year while non-GAAP operating margin remains at or above 34%.
buy_triggers.checkable_at: FY2027 Q1 Form 10-Q and earnings 8-K expected November 2026

buy_triggers.marker: Trailing-four-quarter free cash flow reaches at least $15 billion without annual buybacks falling below $4 billion.

thesis.what_must_be_true: The $9 billion AI-order target must translate into revenue rather than extended-duration backlog, the campus refresh must broaden beyond hyperscalers, and product mix plus restructuring savings must offset tariff and accelerated-infrastructure costs sufficiently to sustain roughly 66% non-GAAP gross margin and mid-30% non-GAAP operating margin.

validated.preview_note: Cisco enters the fiscal-year print with unusually strong networking demand: Q3 product orders rose 35%, networking orders exceeded 50% growth, and management raised FY2026 hyperscaler AI-infrastructure expectations to $9 billion of orders and $4 billion of revenue. I forecast Q4 revenue of $16.86 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.18, producing FY2026 revenue of $62.93 billion and adjusted EPS of $4.29. The principal upside variable is shipment timing against the AI and campus-switching backlog; the principal downside is gross-margin pressure from tariffs and a higher mix of large AI systems. Cash conversion should rebound seasonally, with Q4 free cash flow near $5.0 billion. The reaction should depend less on a modest Q4 beat or miss than on whether FY2027 Q1 guidance confirms continued high-single-digit product momentum. Guidance of at least $15.6 billion with non-GAAP gross margin around 65.5% would support the view that AI and campus demand can carry growth into FY2027; guidance below $15.2 billion or below 65% gross margin would suggest order timing and mix are less favorable than the Q3 order data imply.
validated.reasoning: The Q4 forecast sits $60 million above guidance midpoint because Q3 revenue exceeded guidance while product orders accelerated sharply: total orders grew 35%, orders excluding hyperscalers grew 19%, and networking orders grew more than 50% (0000858877-26-000075, EX-99.1 blocks b0000009-b0000010). GAAP gross margin is modeled at 64.0%, within Cisco's 63.5%-64.5% guidance, with tariffs and AI-system mix preventing a larger sequential recovery. The $450 million restructuring charge follows the amount explicitly identified for Q4 in block b0000173. Adjusted net income of $4,672.8 million divided by 3,960 million diluted shares gives adjusted EPS of $1.18. Q4 operating cash flow of $5.5 billion assumes the inventory build reverses partly and collections strengthen seasonally; after $500 million of capital expenditures, free cash flow is $5.0 billion. Adding the forecast to the filed nine-month results produces FY2026 revenue of $62,933 million, GAAP net income of $12,734.4 million, adjusted EPS of approximately $4.29, operating cash flow of $14,291 million, capex of $1,520 million, and free cash flow of $12,771 million. FY2027 assumes AI backlog conversion and the campus refresh lift revenue approximately 5%, partly offset by softer services and mature collaboration demand. Longer-term distributions widen materially because hyperscaler concentration, Ethernet competition, tariffs, and the durability of enterprise refresh spending create greater uncertainty.
